sources.title: The cost of fast fashion
sources.body: Fast fashion refers to clothing that is designed, produced and sold very quickly and cheaply, allowing retailers to introduce new styles every few weeks. Consumers benefit from low prices, but the environmental costs are considerable. Producing textiles uses large quantities of water and energy, and synthetic fibres such as polyester are made from fossil fuels. Because garments are cheap, they are often worn only a few times before being discarded. Much donated clothing cannot be resold locally and is exported, where a significant share ends up in landfill. Some brands now offer repair services or collect used garments for recycling, but critics argue that the only real solution is to buy fewer, more durable items.

sources.title: What stem cells can do
sources.body: Stem cells are cells that can divide repeatedly and develop into different types of specialised cells, such as muscle, nerve or blood cells. This ability makes them valuable for medical research. Bone marrow transplants, which replace damaged blood-forming cells, have used stem cells successfully for decades. Scientists can also now reprogram ordinary adult cells so that they behave like embryonic stem cells, which avoids some of the ethical concerns associated with using embryos. Researchers hope stem cells will one day help treat conditions such as spinal injuries and heart damage. However, many treatments are still experimental, and some private clinics offer unproven therapies that can be expensive and even dangerous. Patients are advised to seek treatments that are part of properly regulated clinical trials.

sources.title: Restoring wetlands
sources.body: For centuries, wetlands were regarded as wasteland and were drained to create farmland and space for towns. In New Zealand, for example, only a small fraction of the country's original wetlands remain. Scientists now recognise that wetlands provide important services. They filter nutrients and sediment from water before it reaches rivers and lakes, store floodwater during heavy rain and provide habitat for many birds and fish. Restoring a wetland can involve blocking drains, replanting native vegetation and controlling invasive weeds. Some farmers have created small wetlands on their land to improve water quality, and research suggests these can remove a substantial proportion of nitrogen from farm runoff.

sources.title: Electric buses
sources.body: Many cities are replacing diesel buses with electric ones. Electric buses produce no exhaust emissions on the street, which improves air quality, and they are much quieter, making them more pleasant for passengers and residents. Although they are more expensive to buy, they cost less to run, because electricity is usually cheaper than diesel and electric motors need less maintenance. Cities must still overcome practical challenges. Batteries add weight and limit how far a bus can travel before charging, particularly in cold weather or on hilly routes. Depots need new charging equipment and a stronger connection to the grid. Some operators use fast chargers at the end of routes so that buses can top up their batteries during short breaks.

sources.title: How the bicycle changed society
sources.body: The first bicycles of the early nineteenth century had no pedals; riders pushed themselves along with their feet. Later designs with a very large front wheel were fast but dangerous, and they were ridden mainly by young, wealthy men. The development of the safety bicycle in the eighteen eighties, with two wheels of similar size and a chain driving the rear wheel, made cycling far more accessible. Bicycles gave ordinary workers a cheap way to travel longer distances, and they gave many women a new sense of independence. Cycling also encouraged the building of better roads, which later benefited motorists.

sources.title: Making group work work
sources.body: Universities often require students to complete group assignments, partly because employers value the ability to work in teams. Group work can help students develop communication skills and learn from classmates with different backgrounds. Yet many students dislike it. A common complaint is that some members contribute little but receive the same mark as everyone else. Research suggests that the design of the task matters. Groups work better when roles are clearly defined, when the task genuinely requires cooperation, and when individual contributions are assessed as well as the final product. Peer evaluation, in which students rate one another's input, can reduce the problem of unequal effort, although it must be designed carefully to be fair.

sources.title: The role of hydrogen
sources.body: Hydrogen is often described as a clean fuel because using it in a fuel cell produces only water. However, its environmental benefits depend on how it is made. Most hydrogen today is produced from natural gas, a process that releases carbon dioxide. Green hydrogen, made by using renewable electricity to split water, avoids these emissions but is currently more expensive. Hydrogen is also difficult to store and transport, because it is very light and must be compressed or cooled to extremely low temperatures. Many experts believe hydrogen will be most useful in sectors that are hard to electrify, such as steel making, fertiliser production and possibly long-distance shipping, rather than in private cars, where batteries are already more efficient.

sources.title: Breeding crops for drought
sources.body: As droughts become more frequent in many farming regions, plant breeders are working to develop crops that can tolerate dry conditions. Some drought-tolerant varieties have deeper roots that reach water further underground. Others close the small pores on their leaves more quickly to reduce water loss, or complete their growth cycle before the driest part of the season. Breeders use traditional cross-breeding as well as modern genetic techniques that help them identify useful traits more quickly. Traditional crops such as sorghum and millet, which are naturally hardy, are also receiving renewed attention. However, drought-tolerant seeds cannot solve water shortages alone; better soil management and irrigation practices are also essential.

sources.title: Digitising museum collections
sources.body: Most museums can display only a small fraction of their collections at any one time; the rest is kept in storage. Digitisation, which involves photographing or scanning objects and recording information about them, allows people anywhere in the world to explore these hidden collections online. Researchers can compare objects held in different countries without travelling, and teachers can use images in lessons. Digitisation also creates a record that could be valuable if an object is damaged or stolen. However, the process is slow and costly. Each item must be handled carefully, and detailed three-dimensional scans require specialist equipment. Museums must also consider cultural sensitivities, as some communities do not want certain objects to be shared publicly.

sources.title: Loneliness in later life
sources.body: Loneliness is not the same as being alone. A person can live alone and feel content, or be surrounded by others and still feel isolated. Among older adults, loneliness has been associated with poorer physical and mental health, including higher rates of depression and heart disease. Life events such as retirement, the death of a partner or reduced mobility can shrink social networks. Programmes that help often focus on meaningful activity rather than simply bringing people together. Community gardens, volunteering and intergenerational projects, where older adults mentor young people, have shown promising results. Transport also matters, because people who cannot travel easily may lose contact with friends.

sources.title: The problem of space debris
sources.body: Thousands of satellites orbit the Earth, along with far larger numbers of fragments from old rockets, broken satellites and past collisions. Because objects in orbit travel at extremely high speeds, even a small piece of debris can damage a working spacecraft. Space agencies track the larger objects and occasionally move satellites to avoid them. Scientists are concerned about a chain reaction, in which collisions create more fragments that then cause further collisions, making some orbits unusable. Proposed solutions include designing satellites to re-enter the atmosphere and burn up at the end of their missions, and developing spacecraft that can capture and remove debris. International agreement will be needed, since orbits are shared by all nations.

sources.title: Do sugar taxes work?
sources.body: A number of countries have introduced taxes on sugary drinks in an attempt to reduce obesity and tooth decay. The idea is that higher prices will discourage consumption. Evidence from several places suggests that sales of taxed drinks do fall after a tax is introduced. In some cases, manufacturers have also reformulated their products, reducing sugar content to avoid the tax. Critics argue that such taxes are unfair to people on low incomes, who spend a larger share of their income on food and drink. Supporters reply that low-income groups often suffer most from diet-related illness and may therefore benefit most. It is still unclear how much these taxes reduce obesity over the long term, because many other factors affect weight.

sources.title: A predator-free New Zealand
sources.body: New Zealand's native birds evolved without land mammals as predators, so many of them nest on the ground or cannot fly. When humans introduced rats, stoats and possums, bird populations declined dramatically. In response, the country has set a goal of removing these introduced predators by twenty fifty. Offshore islands have already been successfully cleared, allowing species such as the kākāpō to survive. Removing predators from the mainland is far more difficult. It will require new technologies, such as smarter traps and remote monitoring, as well as widespread community support. Some scientists question whether the goal can be fully achieved, but many agree that the effort has already increased protection for native species.

sources.title: What maps reveal
sources.body: Maps are often thought of as neutral descriptions of the world, but historians point out that they also reflect the beliefs and interests of the people who made them. Medieval European maps, for instance, often placed Jerusalem at the centre, expressing a religious view of the world rather than accurate geography. During the age of European exploration, maps recorded new coastlines but also supported claims to territory, sometimes ignoring the people who already lived there. Even modern maps involve choices: which place names to use, which borders to show and which features to emphasise. Reading old maps critically can therefore tell us as much about the past as about geography.

sources.title: Living light
sources.body: Bioluminescence is the production of light by living organisms. It is rare on land, where the best-known examples are fireflies and certain fungi, but it is extremely common in the deep ocean, where sunlight does not reach. Animals use light in many ways. Some attract prey with glowing lures, while others use sudden flashes to startle predators. Certain fish produce light on their undersides that matches the faint light from above, making their outline harder to see from below. In New Zealand, glow-worms in caves such as Waitomo use light to attract small insects into sticky threads. Scientists have also borrowed bioluminescent proteins as tools for tracking processes inside living cells.
